Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Algeria predominantly use paper-based records. Recent analyses (2026) describe public hospitals, including those in rural/southern regions, as largely reliant on handwritten patient folders and notes, with no EHRs at facility level.LinkedIn analysis by health expert. Digital initiatives like DEM.DZ EMR and digital hospitals exist but are pilots (e.g., Annaba wilaya) or hospital-focused, not rolled out to rural clinics.ASJP digital transformation paper. A 2025 rural village study shows low utilization of local primary care due to lack of comprehensive services, with no mention of digital tools.PMC rural access study. DHIS2 listed in old forums but unconfirmed for Algeria; likely aggregate HMIS, not facility-level digital recording. National digital plans aim for zero-paper but rural facilities lag, indicating entirely paper-based at clinics with possible later digitization at higher levels.

revision_notes: Original cited LinkedIn post is accessible and supports the score; the ASJP paper could not be fetched (crawl error) and the PMC study was blocked by a bot-check, so both are treated as unverified rather than confirmed. Fresh searches (2025-2026) confirm rural/primary-care level patient record capture remains overwhelmingly paper-based: an April/May 2026 healthtech market analysis states Algeria's population is served by a health system running 'almost entirely on paper records', with private practitioners (who commonly provide rural primary care) using cardboard folders, handwritten appointment books and photocopied prescriptions. The Ministry of Health's national Dossier Electronique du Patient (DEP) was described as only 'planned for end of 2025' in an October 2025 report and remains a hospital/emergency-care-led rollout that has not reached rural primary clinics. Earlier ministry claims of 90%+ 'digitalisation' of health establishments by mid-2024 appear to describe administrative/connectivity metrics rather than facility-level clinical data capture, and are contradicted by more granular reporting through 2026. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Data capture in Algeria's rural primary healthcare clinics remains overwhelmingly paper-based. Patient records are typically kept in folders and handwritten notes, appointment books are paper-based, and no electronic health record system operates at facility level in the great majority of rural clinics. The government's national Dossier Electronique du Patient initiative, intended to replace paper files with a centralised digital record, was still in the planning and early-rollout phase into 2026, with ministerial calls that spring for 'large-scale digitisation' of the hospital system underscoring that most facilities, including rural and southern clinics, have not yet transitioned to digital record capture. A small and growing number of private clinics use commercial electronic medical record software, but this is not representative of rural primary care provision.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Algeria, primarily Gendarmerie Nationale brigades, record complaints, case files, and incident reports on paper via handwritten procès-verbaux (official records). Official procedure requires victims to present orally at stations where facts are consigned into a PV, then transmitted to prosecutors; digital pre-complaints online require physical signature of PV at the station within 30 days. No evidence of digital recording at rural facilities; later digitization efforts focus on urban justice, traffic fines, or online submissions, not initial rural case logging. Consistent with francophone African norms of paper-based PVs at police/gendarmerie outposts. US State Dept reports detail procedures without mentioning digital tools at station level.
redteam_note: No data year recorded - must be populated during verification.
revision_notes: Original sources (mjustice.gov.dz, an ena.dz gendarmerie PDF, and the US State Department human rights report) could not be fetched directly (403 / timeout errors), so their content is corroborated rather than directly re-verified. A November 2025 platform launched by the Direction Generale de la Surete Nationale (DGSN, the national police) digitises only the declaration of lost, stolen or destroyed documents - an explicitly narrow administrative process - and is run by the urban-focused national police rather than the Gendarmerie Nationale, which polices rural communes under the Ministry of National Defence (per a 2025 UK Home Office country policy note). No evidence was found of digitised initial case-file or incident recording at rural gendarmerie brigades. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural policing in Algeria is primarily undertaken by the Gendarmerie Nationale, whose roughly 1,233 territorial brigades cover rural communes under the Ministry of National Defence. Initial recording of complaints and incidents at these rural posts continues to rely on the handwritten proces-verbal (PV): a citizen must present in person for the facts to be consigned by an officer, and even recently digitised channels for pre-complaints and lost-document declarations either still require a signed paper PV to be produced at the station within a set period, or apply only to the separate, urban-focused national police (DGSN) rather than the rural Gendarmerie. There is no evidence of electronic case-management or incident-recording systems operating at rural station level.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: No direct evidence found on digital data recording at rural primary school level for attendance, enrollment, or grades. National stats from Ministry of Education collected via ONS show aggregates but no methodology indicating school-level digital entry.ONS Education Stats UNESCO report mentions digital platforms for enrollment/results access but pilot digital schools and ICT initiatives focus on access/teaching, not core admin records.UNESCO Algeria Report Rural digital divide noted.Zenodo Rural Digital Divide World Bank notes ICT policy but vast rural areas lagging, implying paper-based collection standard with central aggregation. Evidence points to entirely paper-based at rural facilities, digitized later if at all. Score 1 per rules for broad paper use.

revision_notes: Original ONS/UNESCO/World Bank/Zenodo sources are high-level national statistics and policy reports rather than facility-level evidence and were not re-fetched in full; the underlying claim that rural primary schools capture attendance, enrolment and grades on paper is nonetheless supported by fresher, more specific evidence. A December 2024 field study of electronic administration in Bordj Bou Arreridj primary schools found usage 'limited, with usage confined to specific areas', with organisational, financial and technical obstacles preventing full implementation. National digitisation of first-grade enrolment (announced 2024) is a centralised online registration channel for parents rather than digitisation of in-school record-keeping, and a national tablet programme explicitly favoured schools with single-shift operation and reliable electricity, criteria likely to exclude many rural schools. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Algeria continue to record attendance, enrolment and grades on paper at facility level. National digitisation initiatives launched in 2024 focus on centralising first-grade enrolment through an online portal for parents and on distributing tablets loaded with digital textbooks to a limited number of selected schools (chosen partly on the basis of reliable electricity supply and single-shift operation), rather than on digitising day-to-day administrative record capture within the school itself. Field research into electronic administration in Algerian primary schools found adoption confined to a few specific areas and constrained by infrastructural, financial and organisational barriers, indicating that core facility-level record capture in rural schools remains predominantly paper-based.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Algeria's civil registration (état civil) is managed at commune level, including rural areas, with births declared at the commune of birth. Official Ministry of Interior describes procedures requiring physical presence and documents like livret de famille, suggesting paper-based initial recording by local officers, consistent with traditional registry practices.Ministry of Interior. However, national centralization is advanced: civil registries interconnected since ~2014 allowing extracts from any commune; online 12S secure birth certificate requests via demande12s.interieur.gov.dz; digital birth extracts (نسخة رقمية لشهادة الميلاد) via etatcivil.interieur.gov.dz; biometric integration for passports/ID. US Embassy notes non-acceptance of handwritten certificates, implying printed/digital standard. No direct rural-specific evidence, but central digitization indicates paper at rural points digitized centrally. ECA CRVS reports exclude Algeria but note Africa's rural services often inaccessible/poor quality. Predominantly paper locally with national digital systems/pilots.

revision_notes: Original sources (Ministry of Interior etat civil page, embassy 12S guidance, ecoi.net, US embassy checklist) were reviewed and are broadly consistent but understate the extent of digitisation. Fresh evidence indicates the etat civil registre national has been operating as an automated system since a 2015 decree exempted citizens from presenting physical civil-status documents, with a 2019 Ministry of Interior/ID4Africa presentation confirming over 100 million birth, marriage and death records digitised and communes interconnected for real-time certificate issuance from any commune in under a minute. A May 2023 ministry statement records over 80% of public services, including commune-level civil registry services, delivered online, alongside a national identification number generated automatically from civil status data. However, a November 2023 report on Mascara wilaya shows fibre-optic connections to civil registry annexes still being rolled out at that date (85 town halls connected, several more pending), and southern wilayas retain extended (20-day) declaration windows reflecting continued logistical and connectivity constraints in the most remote communes. This points to most, but not all, rural commune offices now capturing and processing civil status data digitally, with a residual paper component in less-connected areas, consistent with 'Mostly digital - some paper' (3) rather than the previous 'Mostly paper - some digital' (2). This is a moderate promotion, not to the top of the scale, so no escalation is required.
revised_comments: Algeria's civil registry (etat civil) operates as a nationally automated system: a 2015 executive decree exempts citizens from presenting physical civil-status documents because the registre national automatise de l'etat civil now holds authoritative digital records, comprising more than 100 million digitised birth, marriage and death acts. Communes are progressively connected by fibre optic to this national platform, allowing certificates to be issued within minutes from any commune in the country and enabling online retrieval of birth, marriage and death certificates via dedicated portals. As of 2023, government figures indicate over 80% of commune-level public services, including civil status services, are delivered online. Connectivity rollout to some rural annexes was still in progress as of late 2023, and southern wilayas are allowed extended declaration periods reflecting residual logistical constraints in the most remote areas, so a modest proportion of rural registry activity continues to rely on paper processes pending full network coverage.
